To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have prepared a rotaxane consisting a circular DNA and a nucleic acid chain interlocked by hybridization and stoppered by Au NPs, and we demonstrated the switchable fluorescence properties of the rotaxanes.
we have developed an efficient strategy for the preparation of Au NP/DNA rotaxanes and that these supramolecular structures exhibit switchable fluorescence properties.

the rotaxanes can be used to control the position of a fluorophore-modi ed nucleic acid ring by the addition of nucleic acids as fuels and anti-fuels and that the ring transitions can be followed by fluorescence quencing or surface-enhanced flourescence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the preparation of a DNA nanostructure consisting of a circular DNA ring interlocked, through Watson-Crick base-pairing, on a DNA axle and capped by two 10 nm-sized Au NPs.
the development of a novel DNA-based supramolecular system with switchable fluorescence properties and its applications in the construction of functional nanodevices.
the preparation and characterization of a novel hybrid nanostructure and the development of a new method for the reversible switching of the fluorescence properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work provides an important example of the application of DNA nanostructures in the design of novel nanodevices.
a DNA rotaxanes consisting of two 10-nanometer Au NPs and a 10-nanometers long nucleic acid interlocking the two NPs through hybridization, can be switched by the addition of nucleic acids.
the DNA rotaxane hybrid structure is a new class of nanomaterials with switchable fluorescence properties, which can be applied as fluorescent sensors and fluorescent switches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the supramolecular rotaxane is a nanoscopic device that can be switched on and off in a controlled fashion by the addition of specific nucleic acids.

the rotaxane hybrid nanomaterial can be switched between two states reversibly and can be used as a fluorescent sensor for the detection of nucleic acid sequences in the presence of a single base mismatch.
we can control the position of the ring by the fuel-anti-fuel mechanism, which is a novel approach for the construction of a DNA nanoswitch.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNA rotaxane hybrid systems with switchable fluorescence can be used as nanorecorders for the detection and storage of information.
a supramolecular system can be constructed by using DNA as a molecular building block, in which the ring can be switched between two states.
a supramolecular structure can be constructed using DNA as a building block, and the supramolecular assembly can be controlled by the nucleic acid fuel.
